claim: H3K27ac and H3K4me1 signals were reproducible between biological replicates in a region on chromosome 14.
source: H3K27ac and H3K4me1 signals were reproducible between biological replicates as exemplified in a region on chromosome 14 (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and stated in the text.

claim: There was a high correlation between replicates for both H3K27ac and H3K4me1 marks at each age.
source: There was a high correlation between replicates for both marks at each age (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A total of 9,622 peaks were identified by the presence of overlapping peaks between H3K27ac and H3K4me1 at E12, P0, and P9.
source: This highlighted a total of 9,622 peaks; 5,859, 474, and 3,289 peaks that were in both the H3K27ac and H3K4me1 datasets at E12, P0, and P9, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by peak calling data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 7024 active cerebellar enhancers were derived from overlapping H3K27ac and H3K4me1 signals after removing duplicate peaks between ages.
source: Duplicate peaks between ages were removed, producing a list of 7024 active cerebellar enhancers derived from overlapping H3K27ac and H3K4me1 signals (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data processing results described in the text.

claim: An enhancer active at E12 was identified in close proximity to Ascl1.
source: We identified an enhancer active at E12 located in close proximity to Ascl1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A decrease in H3K27ac ChIP-seq signal at the Ascl1 enhancer corresponded to a decrease in Ascl1 gene expression.
source: A decrease in the H3K27ac ChIP-seq signal at this enhancer corresponded to a decrease in Ascl1 gene expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation between ChIP-seq and expression data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Two active enhancers at P9 were identified near Pax6.
source: We identified two active enhancers at P9 located near Pax6 (Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: H3K27ac ChIP-seq signal at Pax6 enhancers showed a pattern of activity similar to Pax6 expression, increasing from embryonic to postnatal ages.
source: H3K27ac ChIP-seq signal also showed a pattern of activity similar to Pax6 expression, increasing from embryonic to postnatal ages (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation between ChIP-seq and expression data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Greater than 90% of robust cerebellar enhancers are replicated by H3K27ac and DNase-seq peaks from Frank et al., 2015.
source: Greater than 90% of our reported robust cerebellar enhancers are replicated by H3K27ac and DNAse-seq peaks from this study (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with previously published data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: 73% of H3K27ac peaks, 59% of H3K4me1 peaks, and 60% of robust cerebellar enhancers overlapped with peaks identified in the adult cerebellum by Gorkin et al., 2020.
source: We found that 73% (7037/9545) of H3K27ac peaks, 59% (20674/35010) H3K4me1peaks and 60% (1974/3289) of robust cerebellar enhancers overlapped with peaks identified in the adult cerebellum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with adult cerebellum data from Gorkin et al., 2020 shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A subset of enhancers identified at P9 are active specifically during postnatal development when compared to adult stages.
source: This indicates that a subset of the enhancers identified at P9 are active specifically during postnatal development when compared to adult stages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overlap analysis showing that not all P9 enhancers are present in adult cerebellum.

claim: 73% and 80% of robust cerebellar enhancers overlapped with the postnatal cerebellum enhancer dataset from EnhancerAtlas 2.0 at P0 and P9, respectively.
source: We found that 73%, and 80% of our enhancers overlapped with the postnatal cerebellum enhancer dataset at P0, and P9, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with EnhancerAtlas 2.0 data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: 56% of VISTA enhancers with hindbrain activity overlap with cerebellar enhancer sequences at E12.
source: We found that 56% of VISTA enhancers overlap with our cerebellar enhancer sequences at E12 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with VISTA Enhancer Browser data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: A higher proportion of H3K27ac peaks overlapped with VISTA enhancers compared to open chromatin regions identified in the developing cerebellum and hindbrain.
source: Additionally, we found that a higher proportion of H3K27ac peaks overlapped with VISTA enhancers compared to open chromatin regions identified in the developing cerebellum (Sarropoulos et al., 2021) and the developing hindbrain (Gorkin et al., 2020; Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative overlap analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: H3K27ac peaks may be more predictive of active enhancers than previously generated chromatin accessibility datasets.
source: This indicates that our identified H3K27ac peaks may be more predictive of active enhancers than previously generated chromatin accessibility datasets.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the higher overlap of H3K27ac peaks with VISTA enhancers compared to chromatin accessibility data.

claim: 89% (6238/7023) of cerebellar enhancers had significant differences in H3K27ac peak signal throughout cerebellar development.
source: The majority, 89% (6238/7023), of cerebellar enhancers had significant differences in peak signal (adjusted P-value ≤0.05) throughout cerebellar development (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At P9, 1273 cerebellar enhancers were significantly active compared to either P0, E12 or both.
source: At P9, 1273 cerebellar enhancers were significantly active compared to either P0, E12 or both.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis results.

claim: At E12, 4432 active enhancers were differentially active compared to either P9, P0 or both.
source: At E12, 4432 active enhancers were differentially active compared to either P9, P0 or both.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis results.

claim: None of the P0 cerebellar enhancers were differentially active when compared to both E12 and P9.
source: However, none of these P0 cerebellar enhancers were differentially active when compared to both E12 and P9, indicating that enhancer activity did not spike at birth.
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis results.

claim: The P0 samples had slightly lower quality control scores on average than the E12 and P9 samples.
source: The P0 samples had slightly lower scores, on average, in both metrics than the E12 and P9 samples, suggesting a minor decrease in sensitivity compared to the other stages.
evidence: The claim is supported by quality control metrics evaluation.

claim: The difference in sensitivity at P0 may have masked P0-specific enhancer activity.
source: We acknowledge that the difference in sensitivity may have masked P0-specific enhancer activity in our analysis and that future experiments may reveal temporally-specific enhancers at this stage.
evidence: The claim is speculative based on quality control metrics.

claim: Two temporally specific windows of enhancer activity were identified at Early (embryonic) and Late (postnatal) stages.
source: Taken together, this analysis highlights two temporally specific windows of enhancer activity at Early (embryonic) and Late (postnatal) stages (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential binding analysis results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Early active enhancers showed a loss of mean H3K27ac signal over time, with a steep decline after E12.
source: For Early active enhancers, there was a loss of mean H3K27ac signal over time, with a steep decline after E12 (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by signal analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Late active enhancers exhibited a gain in activity over time, with mean H3K27ac signal increasing steadily through development.
source: Late active enhancers exhibited a gain in activity over time, with mean H3K27ac signal increasing steadily through development.
evidence: The claim is supported by signal analysis.

claim: The majority of cerebellar enhancers are dynamic throughout time and exhibit temporally specific activity.
source: These results indicate that the majority of cerebellar enhancers are dynamic throughout time and exhibit temporally specific activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential binding analysis results.

claim: The majority of cerebellar H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peaks at E12 overlapped with profiles generated in either the hindbrain, midbrain or forebrain.
source: At E12, we found that the majority of cerebellar H3K27ac and H3K4me1 peaks overlapped with profiles generated in either the hindbrain, midbrain, or forebrain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with other brain regions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At P0, the majority of cerebellar H3K27ac peaks were identified in other brain regions, but only a modest overlap was found for H3K4me1 profiles.
source: Similar results were observed at P0, with the majority of cerebellar H3K27ac peaks identified in other brain regions; however, only a modest overlap was found for H3K4me1 profiles at this stage (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with other brain regions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Most robust cerebellar enhancers overlapped with H3K27ac peaks detected in the hindbrain (89.1%), midbrain (78.6%), or forebrain (78.6%).
source: We found that most robust cerebellar enhancers overlapped with H3K27ac peaks detected in the hindbrain (89.1%), midbrain (78.6%), or forebrain (78.6%; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 69.8% of robust cerebellar enhancers were active in all three developing brain regions (hindbrain, midbrain, and forebrain).
source: When looking at multiple brain regions, 69.8% of robust cerebellar enhancers were active in all three developing brain regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The majority of enhancers active in multiple brain regions (73.9%) were classified as Early active enhancers in the cerebellum.
source: Interestingly, the majority of the enhancers active in these brain regions (73.9%) were classified as Early active enhancers in the cerebellum which display temporally specific activity to embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of enhancer temporal classification and brain region overlap.

claim: 467 (6.7%) robust cerebellar enhancers were specifically active in the cerebellum and not in other brain regions.
source: Importantly, we identified 467 (6.7%) robust cerebellar enhancers specifically active in the cerebellum and not the other brain regions, indicating our analysis has uncovered novel enhancer sequences potentially critical for cerebellar formation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Over half of the cerebellar specific enhancers (55.03%) were classified as Late active enhancers.
source: Over half of the cerebellar specific enhancers (55.03%) were classified as Late active enhancers with activity peaking during postnatal development, while only 15.92% of these enhancers were Early active enhancers and the remaining 29.05% of enhancers were not differentially active (labeled as 'Neither').
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of cerebellar-specific enhancers.

claim: Early enhancers displayed a decrease in average activity over time in the hindbrain, midbrain and forebrain.
source: Early enhancers displayed a decrease in average activity over time in the hindbrain, midbrain and forebrain (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by signal analysis in other brain regions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Late enhancers showed an increase in hindbrain samples, but minimal changes in the developing midbrain and forebrain.
source: Late enhancers showed an increase in hindbrain samples, but minimal changes in the developing midbrain and forebrain (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by signal analysis in other brain regions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Early enhancers may also be active in other developing regions of the brain while Late active enhancers may be more likely to be active specifically in the cerebellum.
source: These collective results indicate that Early enhancers may also be active in other developing regions of the brain while Late active enhancers may be more likely to be active specifically in the cerebellum.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparative analysis of enhancer activity across brain regions.

claim: 6342/7024 (90.1%) robust cerebellar enhancers overlapped with CREs identified by snATAC-seq.
source: We found that 6342/7024 (90.1%) robust cerebellar enhancers overlapped with CREs with open chromatin conformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by overlap analysis with snATAC-seq data from Sarropoulos et al., 2021.

claim: The predicted cell types with the largest proportion of robust cerebellar enhancers were granule cells (19.32%), progenitor cells (18.35%), Purkinje cells (11.48%) and multiple early-born neuron types (9.69%).
source: The predicted cell types with the largest proportion of robust cerebellar enhancers were granule cells (19.32%), progenitor cells (18.35%), Purkinje cells (11.48%) and multiple early-born neuron types (9.69%; Figure 2—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-type assignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The majority of Early enhancers were predicted to be active in progenitor cells and multiple early born neuron types.
source: When splitting cerebellar enhancers into Early and Late active groups, we found that the majority of Early enhancers were predicted to be active in progenitor cells, and multiple early born neuron types such as Purkinje cell precursors while Late enhancers were predicted to be active in developing granule cells, which is the dominant population of cells produced during postnatal stages, and other late-born cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-type assignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Late enhancers were predicted to be active in developing granule cells and other late-born cell types.
source: When splitting cerebellar enhancers into Early and Late active groups, we found that the majority of Early enhancers were predicted to be active in progenitor cells, and multiple early born neuron types such as Purkinje cell precursors while Late enhancers were predicted to be active in developing granule cells, which is the dominant population of cells produced during postnatal stages, and other late-born cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-type assignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Early enhancers peaked in accessibility at embryonic stages and steadily declined throughout developmental time for all cell types.
source: Early enhancers peaked in accessibility at embryonic stages and steadily declined throughout developmental time for all cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Late enhancers gradually increased in accessibility throughout time peaking at postnatal stages for progenitor cells, granule cells and interneurons.
source: Late enhancers gradually increased in accessibility throughout time peaking at postnatal stages for progenitor cells, granule cells and interneurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis.

claim: In Purkinje cells, Late active enhancers showed a minimal change in accessibility throughout time.
source: In Purkinje cells, Late active enhancers showed a minimal change in accessibility throughout time (Figure 2—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by chromatin accessibility analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Early and Late enhancers display their respective activity patterns in the context of chromatin accessibility in individual cell-types.
source: These findings indicate that Early and Late enhancers display their respective activity patterns in the context of chromatin accessibility in individual cell-types.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the chromatin accessibility analysis in different cell types.

claim: HOMER was used to search for enriched motifs in Late and Early active cerebellar enhancers.
source: We used HOMER to search for enriched motifs (adjusted p-value <1E-11) in Late and Early active cerebellar enhancers; which were then matched to known transcription factor motifs in the JASPAR database (Heinz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used for motif enrichment analysis.

claim: A distinct set of significantly enriched motifs was revealed for Early and Late enhancers.
source: This analysis revealed a distinct set of significantly enriched motifs for Early and Late enhancers (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The TFs with the best matching DNA binding motifs belonged to protein families with known regulatory roles in cerebellar development.
source: The TFs with the best matching DNA binding motifs belonged to protein families with known regulatory roles in cerebellar development, serving as validation for our analysis (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis and known TF functions.

claim: TFs enriched in the Early active enhancer group show a decrease in expression over time.
source: TFs enriched in the Early active enhancer group show a decrease in expression over time while TFs enriched in the Late active enhancer group show an increase in expression over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis of TFs with enriched motifs.

claim: TFs enriched in the Late active enhancer group show an increase in expression over time.
source: TFs enriched in the Early active enhancer group show a decrease in expression over time while TFs enriched in the Late active enhancer group show an increase in expression over time.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis of TFs with enriched motifs.

claim: The correspondence between enriched TF expression and enhancer activity provides validation for the findings.
source: This correspondence between enriched TF expression and enhancer activity provides validation for our findings and indicates the timing of enhancer activity may be dictated by the expression and binding of these enriched TFs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between TF expression and enhancer activity.

claim: The timing of enhancer activity may be dictated by the expression and binding of enriched TFs.
source: This correspondence between enriched TF expression and enhancer activity provides validation for our findings and indicates the timing of enhancer activity may be dictated by the expression and binding of these enriched TFs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between TF expression and enhancer activity.

claim: The top three enriched TF motifs for Early active enhancers were Ascl1, Meis2, and Atoh1.
source: The top three enriched TF motifs for Early active enhancers were Ascl1, Meis2, and Atoh1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ascl1, Meis2, and Atoh1 have established roles in cerebellar development, acting as markers of GABAergic or glutamatergic cell types and regulators of differentiation.
source: These TFs have established roles in cerebellar development, acting as markers of GABAergic or glutamatergic cell types and regulators of differentiation (Ben-Arie et al., 1997; Kim et al., 2008; Wizeman et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many of the motifs enriched in the Early group matched with TFs which have received little to no attention in the cerebellum, including Sox4, Lhx2, Rfx4, Pou3f1, and Pax3.
source: Importantly, many of the motifs enriched in the Early group matched with TFs which have received little to no attention in the cerebellum, including Sox4, Lhx2, Rfx4, Pou3f1, and Pax3 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sox4, Lhx2, Rfx4, Pou3f1, and Pax3 have been previously associated with the development of other brain areas.
source: These TFs have been previously associated, however, with the development of other brain areas (Frantz et al., 1994; Porter et al., 1997; Su et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The TFs matching the motifs enriched in the Late active enhancers have a previously identified role in cerebellar development.
source: In contrast, the TFs matching the motifs enriched in the Late active enhancers have a previously identified role in cerebellar development; but not necessarily in the same cellular processes (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The top 3 enriched motifs in Late active enhancers matched with Neurod1, Nfia/b/x, and NF1, which have all been associated with granule cell differentiation.
source: For example, the top 3 enriched motifs matched with Neurod1, Nfia/b/x, and NF1, which have all been associated with granule cell differentiation (Miyata et al., 1999; Sanchez-Ortiz et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by motif enrichment analysis and citations to previous studies.

claim: Pax6 and Smad4 have been found to be critical for granule cell precursor proliferation.
source: However, two other TFs with enriched binding sites, Pax6 and Smad4 have been found to be critical for granule cell precursor proliferation, a process preceding differentiation (Swanson and Goldowitz, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The results suggest a dynamic role for the majority of Early and Late active enhancers, driven by TFs involved in distinct stages of neuron development.
source: These results suggest a dynamic role for the majority of our Early and Late active enhancers, driven by TFs involved in distinct stages of neuron development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the motif enrichment analysis and TF functions.

claim: Pax3 was focused on as a case study because other members of the Pax protein family have been shown to play key roles in the developing cerebellum.
source: As a case study, we focused on Pax3, as other members of the Pax protein family have been shown to play key roles in the developing cerebellum (Leto et al., 2009; Urbánek et al., 1997; Yeung et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies on Pax family members.

claim: Robust Pax3 expression was observed in the ventricular zone (VZ) of the developing cerebellum.
source: We observed robust expression in the ventricular zone (VZ); a neural progenitor region for GABAergic cells in the cerebellum (Leto et al., 2006; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ventricular zone (VZ) is a neural progenitor region for GABAergic cells in the cerebellum.
source: We observed robust expression in the ventricular zone (VZ); a neural progenitor region for GABAergic cells in the cerebellum (Leto et al., 2006; Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Ptf1a is a molecular marker of the VZ and a GABAergic lineage-defining molecule in the cerebellum.
source: A molecular marker of the VZ is Ptf1a, a GABAergic lineage-defining molecule in the cerebellum (Hoshino et al., 2005), and we examined if there was co-expression between Pax3 and Ptf1a.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Colocalization between 50% of Pax3 positive cells in the VZ and Ptf1a was observed.
source: Colocalization between 50% of Pax3 positive cells in the VZ and Ptf1a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), (Hoshino et al., 2005) confirmed Pax3 expression within GABAergic neural progenitors.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent co-staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pax3 expression was confirmed within GABAergic neural progenitors.
source: Colocalization between 50% of Pax3 positive cells in the VZ and Ptf1a (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), (Hoshino et al., 2005) confirmed Pax3 expression within GABAergic neural progenitors.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the colocalization data with Ptf1a.

claim: At E15, Pax3+ cells are seen in the region just dorsal to the VZ, which consist of post-proliferative cells such as Purkinje cells and interneurons.
source: At E15, Pax3 + cells are seen in the region just dorsal to the VZ, which consist of post-proliferative cells such as Purkinje cells and interneurons (Hoshino et al., 2005; Leto et al., 2006; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 4B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Colocalization between 91% of Pax3+ cells and Pax2 was found at E15.
source: While colocalization between 91% of Pax3 + cells and Pax2 was found (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), no co-staining between Pax3 and Foxp2 was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent co-staining data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: No co-staining between Pax3 and Foxp2 was observed at E15.
source: While colocalization between 91% of Pax3 + cells and Pax2 was found (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), no co-staining between Pax3 and Foxp2 was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent co-staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 76% of Pax3+ cells co-localized with Pax2 at P0.
source: We found that 76% of Pax3 + cells co-localized with Pax2 and P0 and that 79% of Pax3 + cells co-localized with Pax2 at P3 (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent co-staining data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 79% of Pax3+ cells co-localized with Pax2 at P3.
source: We found that 76% of Pax3 + cells co-localized with Pax2 and P0 and that 79% of Pax3 + cells co-localized with Pax2 at P3 (Figure 4B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent co-staining data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Pax3 did not colocalize with Calbindin, a Purkinje cell marker, at P0.
source: Pax3 did not colocalize with Calbindin, a Purkinje cell marker, at P0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent co-staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At P9, Pax3 exhibited no observable expression.
source: At P9, Pax3 exhibited no observable expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescent staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Pax3 shows high expression during embryonic stages, peaking at E12, and decreasing steadily after E12.
source: Pax3 shows high expression during embryonic stages, peaking at E12, and decreasing steadily after E12 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by CAGE-seq expression data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Pax3 showed similar expression profiles in the developing mouse and human cerebellum and is highly expressed in Lhx1/5+ GABAergic progenitors and Pax2+ GABAergic interneurons.
source: Pax3 showed similar expression profiles in the developing mouse and human cerebellum and is highly expressed in Lhx1/5+GABAergic progenitors and Pax2 +GABAergic interneurons supporting our immunofluorescent analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-C.

claim: Pax3 expression was also observed in other cell lineages, such as rhombic lip progenitors, UBC/Granule cell progenitors and astrocytes in single-cell data.
source: Pax3 expression was also observed in other cell lineages, such as rhombic lip progenitors, UBC/Granule cell progenitors and astrocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA-seq data.

claim: Pax3 expression in rhombic lip progenitors, UBC/Granule cell progenitors and astrocytes was not observed through immunofluorescent staining, suggesting a misalignment with single-cell data.
source: We do not observe Pax3 expression through immunofluorescent staining in these cell types, which suggests a misalignment with single-cell data.
evidence: The claim is based on the discrepancy between immunofluorescent and single-cell data.

claim: The results indicate that Pax3 is a novel marker for GABAergic progenitors and interneuron precursors in the developing cerebellum.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that Pax3 is a novel marker for GABAergic progenitors and interneuron precursors in the developing cerebellum.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunofluorescent and expression data.

claim: The correlation between H3K27ac signal and gene expression at E12, P0, and P9 was calculated to identify possible gene targets of robust cerebellar enhancers.
source: To identify possible gene targets of our robust cerebellar enhancers, the correlation between H3K27ac signal and mRNA expression of genes located in cis at E12, P0, and P9 was calculated.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used for target gene prediction.

claim: At least one positively correlated target gene was identified for 5815/7023 (70.61%) cerebellar enhancers with an average Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.86.
source: Overall, at least one positively correlated target gene was identified for 5815/7023 (70.61%) cerebellar enhancers with an average Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.86 (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by target gene prediction analysis.

claim: A total of 2261 target genes were identified for robust cerebellar enhancers.
source: In total, we identified 2261 target genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by target gene prediction analysis.

claim: 98 target genes were identified that when knocked out result in a cerebellar phenotype according to the Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI) database.
source: Using the Mouse Genome Informatics (MGI) database, we identified 98 target genes that when knocked out result in a cerebellar phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by database query results.

claim: Cerebellar genes were enriched in putative target genes (p-value = 0.0405).
source: We found that cerebellar genes were indeed enriched in target genes (p-value = 0.0405, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) demonstrating the validity of our high-throughput approach.
evidence: The claim is supported by permutation analysis results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 4 Clusters of co-expressed target genes were identified for Early active enhancers.
source: For Early active enhancers, 4 Clusters of co-expressed target genes were identified (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by k-means clustering analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Genes in Early enhancer clusters had decreasing expression over time, similar to their corresponding enhancer activity.
source: Genes in these clusters had decreasing expression over time, similar to their corresponding enhancer activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis of target genes.

claim: A distinct mean expression profile was observed for each Early enhancer Cluster.
source: However, a distinct mean expression profile was observed for each Cluster (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Genes with known function during cerebellar development showed distinct spatial expression patterns in Early enhancer clusters.
source: Interestingly, genes with known function during cerebellar development showed distinct spatial expression patterns, observed using ISH data from the Developing Mouse Brain Atlas (Thompson et al., 2014; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In Cluster 3, cerebellar genes Ascl1 and Neurog2 are expressed exclusively in the ventricular zone at E11.5.
source: For example, in Cluster 3, cerebellar genes Ascl1 and Neurog2 are expressed exclusively in the ventricular zone at E11.5 while Cluster 4 contains Lhx9 and Meis2 which are expressed in the Nuclear Transitory Zone (neurons destined for the cerebellar nuclei).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Cluster 4 contains Lhx9 and Meis2 which are expressed in the Nuclear Transitory Zone.
source: For example, in Cluster 3, cerebellar genes Ascl1 and Neurog2 are expressed exclusively in the ventricular zone at E11.5 while Cluster 4 contains Lhx9 and Meis2 which are expressed in the Nuclear Transitory Zone (neurons destined for the cerebellar nuclei).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data.

claim: Each Early enhancer cluster is enriched for molecular processes known to be regulated by cerebellar genes within the cluster.
source: A Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis revealed that each cluster is enriched for molecular processes known to be regulated by cerebellar genes within the cluster (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis results shown in Figure 4D.

source: Cells in the ML are Bhlhe22 +may be of two phenotypes: (1) small cell-bodied radially oriented migrating granule cells and (2) larger cell-bodied rounded interneurons.

source: In developing mouse and human cerebellum, Bhlhe22 is highly expressed in granule cells and granule cell progenitors, supporting the results of our immunofluorescent analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

source: Bhlhe22 is also expressed in other cell types in the glutamatergic lineage, such as unipolar brush cells and excitatory cerebellar nuclei as well as high expression in inhibitory GABAergic interneurons neurons indicating importance for both neuronal lineages in the cerebellum.
